period: Late Period to Graeco-Roman, from the 26th Dynasty onward
summary: Three small tombs, three moods: an old priest of Osiris, a doorway guarded by painted cobras, and a yellow crocodile god far from any river.
look: Three tombs on the same hill, usually opened by the same guardian as Si-Amun's. Niperpathot's is the oldest; Mesu-Isis has a frieze of cobras over its doorway; the Crocodile tomb has a long yellow crocodile painted on its wall. They are smaller and plainer than Si-Amun's, so a few minutes in each is enough.
story:
Niperpathot's tomb is probably the oldest decorated tomb on the hill, from the 26th Dynasty, the time when the oracle of Amun was famous across the Greek world. Its owner was a priest, a prophet of Osiris, and the walls carry inscriptions and simple figures, some in faded red ink. It is a reminder that Siwa had its own Egyptian elite long before the Greeks arrived.

The tomb of Mesu-Isis, whose name means 'child of Isis', seems never to have been finished. Its best feature is above the entrance: a frieze of rearing cobras, the uraeus snakes that protected gods and kings, painted in red and blue.

The Crocodile tomb takes its name from the yellow crocodile on its wall: Sobek, the crocodile god, an odd choice in an oasis hundreds of kilometres from the Nile. It belongs to the Greek or Roman period. Like the others, it was rediscovered in 1940, when Siwans took shelter in these tombs during Italian air raids.
details: Mesu-Isis: above the doorway, the row of cobras with raised hoods, still bright in red and blue.
Crocodile tomb: the long yellow crocodile, Sobek, painted on the wall.
Niperpathot: faded red-ink signs and figures; give your eyes a minute to adjust to the dim light.
Compare the faces here with Si-Amun's curly beard: older Egyptian style against Greek taste.
fun_fact: Sobek is a long way from home in Siwa. You will meet him in his own temple at Kom Ombo on the 20th, with real mummified crocodiles next door.
narration: These three smaller tombs on the Mountain of the Dead each have one thing worth your minute. Niperpathot's is probably the oldest decorated tomb here, from the 26th Dynasty, the age of the oracle's fame. Its owner was a priest, a prophet of Osiris, and the walls carry inscriptions and simple figures, some in faded red ink. The tomb of Mesu-Isis, whose name means child of Isis, seems never to have been finished, but above its door runs a frieze of rearing cobras, the snakes that guarded gods and kings, still bright in red and blue. The Crocodile tomb is named after a long yellow crocodile on its wall: Sobek, the crocodile god, a strange guest in an oasis with no river. It belongs to the Greek or Roman period. All three were rediscovered when Siwans sheltered here from bombs in 1940. You will meet Sobek again at his own temple in Kom Ombo on the 20th. For now, step back from the doorway of Mesu-Isis, look up, and count the cobras.

period: Founded 1203; abandoned after the rains of 1926
summary: A whole town of salt and mud, crammed onto a rock behind one gate for centuries, until three days of rain melted it in 1926.
look: Shali is the ruined hill-town in the middle of modern Siwa: a jumble of slumped walls, stairways and window holes, several storeys high, built of kershef. The old mosque with its tapering mud minaret stands at its foot, still in use. Paths lead up through the ruins to viewpoints at the top; come in the late afternoon.
story:
The name means simply 'town' in Siwi. According to local tradition, recorded in the oasis' own chronicle, the Siwan Manuscript, it was founded in 1203. The older settlement at Aghurmi had been weakened by raids, and a small group of families, traditionally seven, moved onto this rock and walled themselves in. They built with kershef: lumps of salty mud from the lake shores that dry as hard as stone, bedded in mud mortar and roofed with palm trunks.

For centuries the town grew upward rather than outward. Houses climbed to four or five storeys, lanes turned into tunnels, and for a long time there was a single gate, shut at night. More gates came later. Families only began to build outside the walls in the 19th century, around 1826 according to tradition.

Kershef has one enemy: rain. Siwa gets about a centimetre a year. But in 1926 it rained for three days, the salt dissolved and walls slumped like candle wax. Families moved to new houses at the foot of the hill, and Shali was left to its old mosque.

Since 2018 a restoration project, with European Union funding and the Egyptian firm Environmental Quality International, has stabilised and rebuilt parts of it using the original materials. The best time to climb is just before sunset, when the walls glow and the call to prayer rises from below.
details: Any wall: look closely for glittering salt crystals and pebbles in the kershef blocks.
Palm-trunk beams poking out of the walls: they once carried floors and roofs.
The old mosque at the foot of the hill, with its tapering mud minaret, still used for prayer.
From the top: Gebel al-Mawta to the north and the two humps of Gebel Dakrur to the south-east.
Restored sections: smoother walls and fresh palm beams, made with the same materials as the originals.
fun_fact: Shali's builders were not foolish: in a place with about a centimetre of rain a year, their salt-and-mud town lasted over 700 years before the storm of 1926 caught up with it.
narration: The crumbling hill in front of you, full of holes like a sponge, is Shali, the old town of Siwa. Its name simply means town in Siwi. According to the oasis' own chronicle, it was founded in 1203, when a few families, traditionally seven, left the older village at Aghurmi after raids and walled themselves in on this rock. They built with kershef: lumps of salty mud from the lake shores that dry as hard as stone, set in mud mortar and roofed with palm trunks. For centuries the town grew upward, not outward. Houses rose four and five storeys, lanes turned into tunnels, and for a long time a single gate was shut every night. Only in the 19th century did families begin to live outside the walls. Kershef has one enemy, rain, and Siwa gets almost none. But in 1926 it rained for three days. The salt dissolved, the walls slumped like candle wax, and the people moved out to new houses below. Since 2018 a restoration project has rebuilt parts of it with the same old materials. As you climb, put your hand on a wall and look closely: you will see glittering salt crystals in the mud. Then, at the top, wait for sunset and the call to prayer from the old mosque below.

period: Ancient spring, perhaps the one Herodotus described in the 5th century BC
summary: A round stone pool bubbling with spring water, named after a queen who never came here, and perhaps the 'Fountain of the Sun' of Herodotus.
look: A circular, stone-lined pool of clear water beside the road from Siwa town toward Aghurmi. Look down and you will see strings of bubbles rising from the spring in its floor. Cafés and changing cabins stand around it, and water runs off in channels into the palm gardens.
story:
Cleopatra never came to Siwa, and no ancient source links her to this pool; the name is a modern one for visitors. Siwans call it Ain Guba, often explained as the Spring of Juba. If that is right, it may remember Juba II, the scholar-king of Mauretania who wrote a book on Libya and married Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony. So there may be a Cleopatra in the story after all, one generation down.

Herodotus describes a spring at the sanctuary of Ammon that he calls the Fountain of the Sun: lukewarm at dawn, colder as the morning goes on, very cold at noon, then warmer again until it boils at midnight. The likely explanation is simple. Spring water keeps one temperature all day, so it feels cold in the midday heat and warm in the chilly desert night. Whether this pool or another near the temple was his fountain, nobody can prove.

This is a local spring as well as a tourist stop. Men swim in shorts; women usually swim in leggings and a T-shirt, or choose a more private pool at a hotel or in the desert.
details: Bubbles rising from the floor of the pool: the spring itself pushing up through the rock.
The stone rim: where local boys jump in.
Channels leading off from the pool into the palm gardens: the spring still waters the farms.
The cafés around the edge: a mint tea or a date drink after your swim.
fun_fact: Herodotus was told this kind of spring boiled at midnight. The water never changed; the people dipping their hands in did.
narration: This round stone pool is Cleopatra's Spring. Cleopatra never came to Siwa, and no ancient writer links her to it; the name is a modern one for visitors. Siwans call it Ain Guba, often explained as the Spring of Juba. If so, it may remember Juba the Second, a king of Mauretania who wrote about Libya and married Cleopatra Selene, the daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony. So there may be a Cleopatra here after all, one generation down. Herodotus wrote of a spring by the sanctuary of Ammon, the Fountain of the Sun: lukewarm at dawn, very cold at noon, and boiling by midnight. The real trick is simpler. Spring water stays at one temperature all day, so it feels cold in the midday heat and warm on a chilly desert night. This pool may be his fountain, or another nearby; nobody can prove which. If you swim, men wear shorts, and women usually swim in leggings and a T-shirt. Now look down into the water: those strings of bubbles rising from the floor are the spring itself.

summary: A two-humped hill where Siwans bury themselves in hot sand to cure aching joints, and where the oasis eats together once a year to make peace.
look: Gebel Dakrur rises a few km south-east of Siwa town: a rocky hill with two humps and sandy slopes at its foot. The shallow pits in the sand are the summer sand baths, with simple shelters nearby where patients rest. From the slopes you look back over the palms to Shali and the salt lakes.
story:
In July and August, when the sand is at its hottest, the hill becomes an open-air clinic. A patient lies in a shallow pit and is covered with sun-heated sand up to the neck, head shaded, for a short session, then wrapped up and rested in a tent with hot drinks. Siwans swear by it for rheumatism and aching joints, and people come from across Egypt for a course of several days. By October the season is over, but the pits are often still visible.

The hill is also the stage for Siwa's great festival, the Siyaha. Each autumn, around the full moon, the men of the oasis gather on Dakrur for three days. They pray, chant Sufi hymns and eat together from shared dishes, rich and poor side by side, and old quarrels are supposed to be settled before anyone goes home. The festival honours the local saint Sidi Sulayman, and visitors often call it the festival of reconciliation.

In 2026 the October full moon falls around the 26th, after you leave, but the dates are set locally, so ask.
details: At the foot of the hill: shallow trenches in the sand, the summer sand baths.
Simple huts and shelters near the pits, where patients rest after a session.
The two humps of the hill: once you know the shape, you will spot Dakrur from all over the oasis.
From the slopes, look north-west: Shali and the town, with Gebel al-Mawta beyond.
fun_fact: Siwa may be the only place in Egypt where the doctor's waiting room is a sand pit, and the treatment is free sunshine.
narration: The two-humped hill in front of you is Gebel Dakrur, and it has two jobs. In July and August, when the sand is at its hottest, it is Siwa's open-air clinic. Patients are buried up to the neck in shallow pits of sun-heated sand, with their heads in the shade, then wrapped up and rested in a tent with hot tea. Siwans swear by it for rheumatism and aching joints, and people come from all over Egypt for a course of several days. Its other job is peace. Every autumn, around the full moon, the men of the oasis gather here for the Siyaha festival. For three days they pray, chant Sufi hymns and eat together from shared dishes, rich and poor side by side, and old quarrels are supposed to be settled before anyone goes home. In 2026 the October full moon falls around the 26th, just after you leave, but dates are set locally, so ask. Now look at the foot of the hill for the shallow trenches in the sand: those are the sand baths.

summary: A palm island on a salt lake, a café facing west, and Siwa's favourite sunset, with a quiet lesson about too much water in the desert.
look: Fatnas is a palm-covered island on the shore of Birket Siwa, the big salt lake west of town, now reached by a causeway. Walk through the palms to the café on the western shore and face the water: the sun sets over the lake.
story:
Its nickname is Fantasy Island, and it has one job: sunset. Find a seat, order tea, and watch the lake turn silver, then gold, then pink as the sun goes down behind the far shore.

The lake itself tells a less pretty story. Siwa has no outlet to the sea, so all the water from its springs and wells that plants do not use or the sun does not evaporate drains into the low salt lakes, carrying salt with it. As more wells were drilled in recent decades, more water arrived than the sun could remove. The lakes spread, groundwater under the gardens rose, and salt crept into the soil; some palm groves near the shores have drowned. In one of the driest places on earth, Siwa's big environmental problem is too much water.
details: Dead palm trunks standing in the shallows along the shore: groves drowned by the rising lake.
The white salt crust along the water's edge.
The café terrace facing west: arrive half an hour before sunset for a front-row seat.
Water birds feeding in the shallows at dusk.
fun_fact: Siwa gets about a centimetre of rain a year, and its biggest headache is still too much water.
narration: You are on Fatnas, a palm-covered island on the shore of Birket Siwa, the salt lake west of town, now joined to the land by a causeway. People come here for one thing: sunset. Take a seat at the café, order mint tea, and face west across the water. As the sun drops, the lake turns silver, then gold, then pink. The lake also tells a quieter story. Siwa has no outlet to the sea. Every drop from its springs and wells that is not used by plants or dried by the sun drains into these low salt lakes. Since many new wells were drilled in recent decades, more water has been arriving than the sun can evaporate. The lakes have spread, the groundwater under the gardens has risen, and salt has crept into the soil. So, in a place with almost no rain, the big problem is too much water. Now look along the shore for dead palm trunks standing in the shallows: trees the rising lake has drowned.

summary: Turquoise pools so salty you float like a cork, cut into a lake bed that supplies salt for building, eating and export.
look: The pools lie beside the salt workings on the edge of one of the big lakes, a short drive from town: basins of vivid turquoise water over a white floor, edged with snow-white crust. Mounds of harvested salt and machinery stand nearby. Bring sandals, a towel and a bottle of fresh water.
story:
Siwa sits in a closed basin. Water from its springs and gardens drains into the low salt lakes, chiefly Birket Siwa west of town and Birket Zeitoun to the east, and the desert sun evaporates it, leaving the salt behind. Over centuries thick white crusts have built up along their shores.

That salt is a resource. Siwans built Shali from salty kershef, and today salt is mined commercially from the lake beds, refined and trucked out of the oasis; much of it is reportedly exported. Shops in town sell carved salt lamps, candle holders and blocks.

The swimming pools are a by-product of the mining: basins cut into the crust that filled with brine far saltier than the sea. Clear water over a white salt floor gives the colour, and the salt makes you float without trying, as in the Dead Sea.

A few rules. Do not shave the day before. Keep the water out of your eyes and any cuts. Wear sandals, because the crust is sharp. Rinse with fresh water afterwards, or the salt dries into a white crust on your skin.
details: The pool edges: salt growing in white plates and knobbly shapes. Beautiful, and sharp underfoot.
The colour: turquoise over the white salt floor, deepening to blue where the pool is deeper.
Mounds of harvested salt and machinery at the nearby works: industry on an old lake bed.
Your skin after the swim: a fine white crust as the brine dries in the sun.
fun_fact: You float here just as in the Dead Sea, which lies more than 400 metres below sea level; Siwa manages it at only about 18 metres down.
narration: These turquoise pools are a by-product of salt mining. Siwa sits in a closed basin with no outlet. Water from its springs and gardens drains into the low salt lakes, Birket Siwa to the west and Birket Zeitoun to the east, and the desert sun evaporates it, leaving salt behind in thick white crusts. Siwans built their old town, Shali, from salty mud, and today the salt is mined from the lake beds, refined and sent out of the oasis, much of it reportedly abroad. Where basins were cut into the crust, they filled with brine far saltier than the sea, over a snow-white floor, and that is what gives the water this colour. Get in and you will float without trying, as in the Dead Sea. A few rules: wear sandals, because the crust is sharp, keep the water out of your eyes and any cuts, and bring fresh water to rinse off afterwards. Now look at the edge of the pool: the salt grows in white plates and knobbly shapes, like coral made of crystal.

summary: Egypt's only Berber-speaking community: a language that is almost never written, silver bridal discs, embroidered dresses and some of Egypt's best dates.
look: The House of Siwa Museum, near Shali, is a traditional kershef house furnished with Siwan clothes, silver jewellery, baskets and pottery: a quick way to see what the market sells and what the old life looked like. The market square below Shali has dates, olive oil, baskets, embroidered shawls and silver.
story:
Most Siwans are Amazigh, or Berbers, and among themselves they speak Siwi, the easternmost Berber language, a relative of dialects spoken in Libya. Estimates run from about 15,000 to 21,000 speakers. Siwi is hardly ever written; Siwans write in Arabic, and their own language lives in songs, riddles, poems and proverbs. Nearly everyone also speaks Egyptian Arabic, and UNESCO lists Siwi as definitely endangered.

To keep the old way of building and living from vanishing, a traditional house was rebuilt as the House of Siwa Museum, around 1990, an idea usually credited to a Canadian diplomat. Inside is the silver that once made a bride's fortune: the adrim, a large silver disc, and the aghraw, a heavy round necklace. A wealthy bride's full set could weigh 5 to 6 kg. Since the road arrived, gold has largely replaced silver, but embroidery survives on dresses and shawls.

Women are rarely seen in public, and outside the home they wrap themselves in the tarfottet, a grey-blue shawl whose cloth comes from Kirdasa near Giza. Historically the gardens were worked and guarded by young unmarried men, the zaggala, a name usually explained as 'club bearers', remembered for their songs, dances and palm wine.

Dates are the economy: Siwa's date farming was added to the UN FAO's list of agricultural heritage systems in 2016, and olive oil is the second crop. In the market, bargaining is expected but gentle; a smile works better than a hard line.
details: In the House of Siwa: the big silver adrim disc and heavy necklaces in the jewellery display.
Embroidered shawls and dresses: dense stitching in bright colours, a Siwan speciality.
In the market: dates soft and dry; ask to taste two kinds before you buy.
The grey-blue tarfottet worn by women passing in donkey carts. Remember: no photos.
Baskets of palm fibre, often with coloured trim: an old Siwan craft still made today.
fun_fact: Siwi borrowed almost all its numbers from Arabic: only 'one' and 'two' are still Berber.
narration: The people around you are mostly Amazigh, or Berbers, and this is the only Berber-speaking community in Egypt. Among themselves they speak Siwi, the easternmost Berber language in the world, related to dialects in Libya. Perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people speak it. It is almost never written: Siwans write in Arabic, and Siwi lives in songs, riddles and proverbs. A nice detail: it borrowed nearly all its numbers from Arabic, and only one and two are still Berber. Until the road came in the 1980s, the oasis lived by its own rules. Brides wore a fortune in silver, a big disc called the adrim and heavy necklaces, sometimes 5 or 6 kilos in all. The House of Siwa Museum, a traditional salt-mud house, keeps pieces like these, with embroidered dresses, baskets and pottery. Siwa is conservative. Women rarely appear in public, and when they do, they are wrapped in a grey-blue shawl called the tarfottet. Please do not photograph women, and ask men first. In the market, dates are king: there are hundreds of thousands of palms here, plus excellent olive oil. Bargain, but gently. Now look at the dates on offer and ask to taste two kinds, a soft one and a dry one: the difference will surprise you.

summary: Egypt's great hollow sinks to 133 metres below sea level, and someone once proposed flooding it using 213 nuclear explosions.
look: You will not see Qattara from the Siwa road; it lies off to the east. What you do see are its smaller cousins: white, cracked salt flats and marshy hollows below the escarpment as the road drops into the Siwa depression, about 18 to 19 metres below sea level.
story:
Siwa lies in a chain of desert hollows scooped out by wind and salt. The biggest, the Qattara Depression, covers about 19,600 square kilometres and reaches 133 metres below sea level, the second-lowest point in Africa. Its floor of salt pans and soft salt marsh stopped tanks, which is why it protected the southern flank at El Alamein in 1942.

Since 1912 engineers have dreamed of letting the Mediterranean pour in to make hydroelectric power. A German scheme of the 1970s proposed digging the channel with 213 nuclear explosions. Egypt said no.

Siwa's own water does not come from the sea. It rises from deep sandstone layers under the Western Desert, filled by rain that fell thousands of years ago, which is why springs bubble up in the middle of a desert.
details: On the drive in: white salt crust and cracked mud flats in the low ground near the road.
The escarpment where the road descends: the rim of the Siwa depression.
Your phone's GPS altitude as you enter the oasis: watch it slip below zero.
fun_fact: The flooding plan would have used 213 hydrogen bombs to dig one canal; Egypt, wisely, declined.
narration: On the drive into Siwa you go below sea level. The oasis floor lies about 18 to 19 metres down, in one of a chain of desert hollows carved out by wind and salt. The biggest is the Qattara Depression, east of here, which reaches 133 metres below sea level, the second-lowest point in Africa. Since 1912 engineers have dreamed of letting the Mediterranean pour into it to make electricity, and one plan in the 1970s proposed digging the canal with 213 nuclear explosions. Egypt said no. Siwa's water does not come from the sea. It rises from deep sandstone layers, filled by rain that fell thousands of years ago. Look out for the white, cracked salt flats by the road: that is water evaporating.
